body:
Formation of Gujarat and the early development strategy

The State of Gujarat was formed on 1 May 1960 under the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960. The former Bombay State was reorganised into Gujarat and Maharashtra.

Gujarat inherited a significant commercial and industrial tradition, including textile manufacturing in Ahmedabad, trade centres, agricultural production and coastal trading activities. After state formation, development efforts included industrial infrastructure, irrigation, agriculture, cooperatives, transport, power supply, education and health services.

These activities developed within India's broader mixed-economy framework. Government institutions and private businesses both contributed to Gujarat's economy well before the national reforms of 1991.

Important institutions and policy milestones

YearInstitution or eventSignificance
1960Formation of GujaratCreation of a separate state administration
1962Gujarat Industrial Development CorporationDevelopment of industrial estates and infrastructure
1982Gujarat Maritime BoardDevelopment and regulation of the state's non-major ports
1991National economic reformsGreater scope for trade, investment and competition
1995Gujarat Port PolicyGreater private participation in port development
1997Gujarat BOOT port policyFramework for private investment in specified port projects

Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation

The Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation (GIDC) was established in 1962 under the Gujarat Industrial Development Act, 1962.

GIDC develops industrial estates by identifying suitable land, planning industrial areas, allotting plots and providing supporting infrastructure. Industrial estates can offer roads, water supply, electricity arrangements and other common facilities required by enterprises.

Such infrastructure can reduce the practical difficulties faced by firms establishing factories. It can also encourage industrial clusters, where related producers, suppliers, workers and service providers operate near one another.

GIDC is a state-level institution. It is not the same as the Gujarat Maritime Board, which is associated with non-major ports and maritime development.

How the 1991 reforms affected states

Before liberalisation, many investment decisions were heavily influenced by central industrial licensing and restrictions. As more industries were opened to private investment and international markets, the availability of suitable locations and infrastructure became increasingly important.

States could seek to attract investment by improving:

  • Industrial land and infrastructure.
  • Transport connections to domestic markets and ports.
  • Reliability of electricity and other essential services.
  • Administrative procedures and investment facilitation.
  • Education, skills and the availability of workers.

This is one form of competitive federalism: states seek to improve their economic and administrative performance, partly by competing to attract investment and employment.

Cooperative federalism involves the Union and states working together on shared development objectives. The 2 ideas are compatible. A state may compete to attract a new factory while cooperating with the Union on highways, education, health or infrastructure projects.

Competition among states does not mean that every state controls all economic policies. International trade policy, customs duties and monetary policy are primarily national responsibilities, while states influence many location-specific conditions such as industrial infrastructure, land administration and local public services.

Why Gujarat attracted industrial activity

Gujarat's industrial development reflects the combination of several factors: established commercial networks, manufacturing experience, access to the Arabian Sea, ports, transport connections, industrial estates and investment in infrastructure.

Some sectors, such as textiles and cooperative dairying, had strong foundations before 1991. Later economic reforms increased opportunities for other activities, including internationally connected manufacturing, petroleum processing and private port development.

It would therefore be incorrect to attribute Gujarat's entire industrial history to the 1991 reforms. The state combined older industrial and cooperative foundations with new opportunities created by liberalisation.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarat was formed on 1 May 1960 under the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960.
  • GIDC was established in 1962.
  • Gujarat Maritime Board was established in 1982.
  • Gujarat introduced its Port Policy in 1995 and BOOT port policy in 1997.
  • Competitive federalism involves competition among states to improve performance.
  • Trap: Gujarat's industrialisation and cooperative movement both began before the 1991 reforms.

[Sources: Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960, sections 2–3; Government of Gujarat, 'History of Gujarat', official state portal; Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation, FAQ, 'What is GIDC?' and 'Functions/activities'; Gujarat Maritime Board, 'Greenfield Ports', sections on the 1995 Port Policy and 1997 BOOT policy; NITI Aayog, 'Competitive Federalism' (official websites consulted 23 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Gujarat's institutional timeline spans both sides of the 1991 national reforms, with competitive and cooperative federalism explained below.
pictures.caption: Gujarat's institutional development began before economic liberalisation and continued after it.

title: Gujarat's Development Trajectory since 1960 and Competition among States

body:
Agriculture in Gujarat's development

Agriculture has remained important to Gujarat's rural economy throughout the period after 1960. It supplies food, raw materials for industry and livelihoods for farmers, agricultural labourers and workers in related activities.

Gujarat's agricultural conditions differ considerably between regions. Rainfall, irrigation, soils and access to markets influence which crops are grown and how reliably farmers can produce them.

Important crops and agricultural regions

  • Cotton: An important commercial crop that supplies the textile industry. Cotton cultivation is significant in several parts of Gujarat, including Saurashtra.
  • Groundnut: A major oilseed crop associated particularly with Saurashtra. Production can be affected by variations in monsoon rainfall.
  • Castor and other oilseeds: Important commercial crops in suitable parts of Gujarat, including areas of north Gujarat.
  • Rice and sugarcane: Grown in areas where rainfall or irrigation provides sufficient water, including parts of south and central Gujarat.
  • Bajra and other relatively drought-tolerant crops: Important in drier agricultural conditions.
  • Animal husbandry: Provides milk, livestock products and supplementary income, including in areas where crop production is vulnerable to rainfall variation.

A commercial crop is grown mainly for sale and income. However, a crop such as cotton or groundnut is not grown exclusively for export. It may supply domestic industries and markets as well.

Irrigation and agricultural development

Gujarat contains regions with relatively limited or variable rainfall. Irrigation can reduce dependence on the monsoon, support additional cropping and improve the reliability of agricultural production.

The Sardar Sarovar Project on the Narmada River and its canal network have played an important role in expanding water infrastructure. The Ukai project on the Tapi River is another important water resource project associated with irrigation and other uses.

Canal irrigation and groundwater irrigation have different characteristics. Canal systems distribute water through constructed channels, while groundwater irrigation uses wells and borewells. Excessive groundwater extraction can reduce water levels, especially where recharge is limited.

Irrigation also has limits. Its benefits depend on actual water availability, distribution, maintenance and suitable farming practices. Large water projects may also involve environmental effects and the displacement or rehabilitation of affected communities.

From agricultural production to cooperative marketing

Many small producers find it difficult to bargain individually with large buyers or intermediaries. A cooperative is an organisation in which members join together to pursue a common economic purpose, generally through shared ownership and collective decision-making.

Cooperatives can organise procurement, provide inputs, process products and improve access to markets. Their effectiveness depends on good management, member participation and financial discipline.

The Anand dairy cooperative model

The dairy cooperative movement centred on Anand has special importance in Gujarat's economic history.

The cooperative associated with the Amul movement began in 1946 in the former Kaira district. Milk producers organised collectively to improve their bargaining position and reduce dependence on private intermediaries. Tribhuvandas Patel played an important leadership role in its establishment, while Verghese Kurien later made major contributions to professional management and the wider dairy development movement.

The cooperative system became known as the Anand Pattern. It uses a 3-tier institutional structure.

LevelInstitutionMain role
VillageMilk producers' cooperative societyCollects milk from members
DistrictDistrict cooperative milk producers' unionProcesses milk and provides producer services
StateState cooperative milk marketing federationCoordinates marketing of products from member unions

The model helps connect small producers with processing facilities, veterinary services, organised marketing and consumers. Payments based on milk quantity and quality provide a link between individual production and collective marketing.

NDDB, Operation Flood and the White Revolution

The National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) was established in 1965 at Anand. It helped extend organised dairy development and the cooperative model to other parts of India.

Operation Flood was launched in 1970 to expand milk production, improve rural incomes and supply milk to consumers through organised networks.

The programme was implemented in 3 phases:

  • Phase I: 1970–1980.
  • Phase II: 1981–1985.
  • Phase III: 1985–1996.

The Gujarat Cooperative Milk Marketing Federation (GCMMF) was established in 1973 and markets dairy products under brands including Amul.

The expansion of dairy production and cooperative marketing is associated with India's White Revolution. This must be distinguished from the Green Revolution, which involved major improvements in crop production through high-yielding varieties, irrigation, fertilisers and related agricultural practices.

Green Revolution: Primarily associated with crop productivity, especially foodgrains. White Revolution: Associated with milk production and dairy development. The Anand Pattern is a cooperative organisational model; Operation Flood was a national dairy development programme.

Agriculture after liberalisation

Greater integration with markets can create opportunities for farmers to sell commercial crops and processed products. However, prices may become more sensitive to international demand, imports and changing production costs.

For small farmers, better irrigation, storage, transport, agricultural credit, cooperatives and access to information can be as important as access to a larger market.

Gujarat's experience demonstrates that agricultural development involves more than increasing crop output. Processing, animal husbandry, cooperative organisation and market connections also shape rural livelihoods.

Prelims focus

  • The Amul cooperative movement originated at Anand in 1946.
  • NDDB was established in 1965 at Anand.
  • Operation Flood was launched in 1970.
  • GCMMF was established in 1973.
  • The Anand Pattern has village, district and state-level cooperative institutions.
  • Trap: Operation Flood concerns dairy development, not the Green Revolution in crop agriculture.

[Sources: NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, ch. 5, 'Land Resources and Agriculture', pp. 40–47; Government of Gujarat, 'History of Gujarat', section on agriculture; National Dairy Development Board, 'Genesis', 'Operation Flood' and 'The Anand Pattern'; National Dairy Development Board, 'Cooperative Dairying Movement'; Amul, 'CRISIL Rating for GCMMF', section 'About the Federation' (official websites consulted 23 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Farmers deliver milk in metal containers to a village cooperative collection centre in 1970s rural Gujarat.
pictures.caption: Milk collection through village cooperatives became a major feature of Gujarat's rural development.

pictures.alt: Milk moves from producers through village collection to district processing; the producer-owned state federation coordinates marketing. GCMMF began in 1973.
pictures.caption: The Anand Pattern connects village milk producers with district processing and state-level marketing.

title: Agriculture, Irrigation and the Dairy Cooperative Movement in Gujarat

body:
From established industries to diversified manufacturing

Gujarat had important commercial and manufacturing centres before becoming a separate state in 1960. Ahmedabad was historically associated with cotton textiles, while other centres developed industries based on agriculture, trade, chemicals and engineering.

After 1960, industrial estates, electricity, transport and market connections supported the expansion of manufacturing. Following the 1991 reforms, producers gained additional opportunities through private investment, access to technology and international markets.

Gujarat's development was not limited to one industry. Different regions became associated with different types of manufacturing.

Important industrial centres

Centre or regionImportant industrial associationRelevant connection
AhmedabadTextiles and diversified manufacturingEstablished industrial and commercial base
SuratDiamond cutting and polishing; textilesProcessing, trade and export markets
JamnagarPetroleum refining and related industriesPort access and large-scale processing
VadodaraEngineering, chemicals and petrochemicalsIndustrial infrastructure and established enterprises
Ankleshwar, Bharuch and DahejChemicals and petrochemicalsIndustrial estates, transport and port facilities
RajkotEngineering and manufacturing enterprisesIndustrial skills and supplier networks
MorbiCeramicsConcentration of specialised manufacturing units
SanandAutomobiles and associated manufacturingIndustrial investment and supplier development

These are important industrial associations, not exclusive classifications. Cities may support many industries, and the location of a particular factory can differ from the main centre traditionally associated with its industry.

Why industries concentrate in particular places

The location of manufacturing depends on the requirements of production. Important factors include raw materials, labour, electricity, water, land, capital, transport and markets.

Different industries depend on these factors to different degrees. Cotton textiles can benefit from access to cotton, workers, markets and transport. Petroleum refining requires facilities for obtaining crude oil, large processing plants and systems for transporting petroleum products.

A concentration of similar or connected enterprises is called an industrial cluster. Clusters can develop specialised workers, suppliers, transport services and commercial networks. These shared advantages may attract additional businesses.

The role of GIDC

The Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation (GIDC) supports industrial development by providing planned industrial areas and supporting facilities. A manufacturer locating in an industrial estate may benefit from established roads, utility connections and proximity to other enterprises.

This is different from the government itself manufacturing every product. A state agency can provide infrastructure while production is carried out by private or public enterprises.

Gujarat's industries and globalisation

The link between Gujarat's industries and international markets can be understood through 2 important examples.

Diamond processing in Surat

Rough diamonds may be imported into India for cutting and polishing. Skilled workers and specialised enterprises in Surat transform the stones into finished products that can be sold in international markets.

This activity illustrates value addition: the processing stage increases the commercial value of the material. It also demonstrates how an Indian manufacturing centre can participate in an international production chain.

However, demand for polished diamonds depends partly on conditions in foreign markets. A decline in international demand may affect local enterprises and employment.

Petroleum refining around Jamnagar

Petroleum refineries process crude oil into products such as fuels and other petroleum-based materials. Access to maritime transport is important where large quantities of crude oil are imported.

Refining activity also supports connected industries, transport operations and other economic services. The supply chain may involve international imports, processing within Gujarat and sales in domestic or international markets.

Industrial benefits and associated challenges

Industrial development can generate employment, increase production, create demand for transport and other services, and support the growth of towns and cities.

At the same time, industrial expansion can create pressure on land, water and electricity. Chemical industries require appropriate waste management and pollution control. Workers also need safe conditions, suitable skills and access to essential services.

Therefore, industrial success cannot be assessed only by the number of factories or the value of industrial output. Employment quality, environmental protection and the distribution of benefits are also important.

Prelims focus

  • Ahmedabad is historically associated with cotton textiles.
  • Surat is an important centre for diamond cutting, polishing and textiles.
  • Jamnagar is associated with petroleum refining.
  • Morbi is associated with ceramics.
  • GIDC supports industrial development through industrial estates and infrastructure.
  • Trap: An industrial cluster is a concentration of related economic activities, not necessarily a single government-owned factory.

[Sources: NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, ch. 8, 'Manufacturing Industries', pp. 85–103; Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation, FAQ, sections on industrial estates and infrastructure; NITI Aayog, Export Preparedness Index 2024, Gujarat industrial and export-cluster discussion (consulted 23 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Workers operate textile machinery and inspect patterned fabric in a modern manufacturing workshop in Surat, Gujarat.
pictures.caption: Surat's textile industry illustrates the importance of manufacturing skills and specialised industrial centres.

pictures.alt: Imported crude oil arrives through Gujarat's ports, is refined at Jamnagar, and becomes petroleum products for domestic markets or export.
pictures.caption: Petroleum refining links imported raw materials, industrial processing and domestic or international markets.

title: Industrial Development, Manufacturing Clusters and International Trade in Gujarat
